paragraphs: News of the withdrawal from the Fei River reached Chang’an before the Qin army had even passed Luoyang.

It came first to the Secretariat, sealed inside a black-lacquered bamboo tube. The courier’s horse was crusted white with dried sweat; even after passing through the Chengming Gate, its four legs still trembled. The tube held a single sheet, written in a careful hand: The camps on the Huai have withdrawn north as ordered; baggage trains have preceded the troops; the several commands remain in good order; the Jin army has made no attack. At the foot stood the seals of the imperial camp and the Central Army Office.
The men at the Department of State Affairs began copying it into the customary form of a victory dispatch. But when the young clerk reached the words “triumphant return,” his brush stopped.
“If there was no battle, can we call it a triumph?”
The senior clerk in charge of the file said, “The dispatch never used those words. Copy it as written.”

By the time the military report was posted outside the East Market, the two deleted words had already made the rounds of Chang’an’s wine shops. Some said Xie Xuan had frightened a hundred and fifty thousand Qin soldiers into retreat. Some said the Heavenly King had seen the Jin army across the Fei and lost his nerve. Others described, in convincing detail, a slaughter that had never happened, even down to the way the Qin troops had supposedly flung away their helmets and armor.
But the doors of the Deng family’s leather shop in the South Market were shut.

Deng Qian had borrowed heavily against the campaign, buying so much cattle hide before autumn that the stacks reached the roof beams. A procurement officer from the army had told him Luoyang would require winter clothing. Deng had persuaded his wife to pawn her gold hairpin and hired twenty craftsmen to make leather boots. Now the army was coming home, the procurement officer had disappeared, and creditors beat on the door more often than the watch drums sounded news of victory.
At dawn on the third day, they found Deng Qian dead in his own well.

His wife, Madam Cao, tucked the procurement note he had left among their contracts and went to seek a hearing at the Department of State Affairs. Autumn wind shook strands of hair loose about her face. She sat beneath the steps all day without weeping or making a scene. Not until the offices were about to close did a clerk emerge to tell her that, lacking the seals of the Secretariat and the army, the note could not count as an official contract.
“I can read,” Madam Cao said. “It says six thousand pairs of boots. The officer even ate at our table.”
The clerk had no answer. He told her she could bring a charge before the Court of Justice against the officer for making unauthorized promises of military purchases.
She gripped the ring of the office door. “If I win my case, will anyone buy the leather in my house?”

The question traveled the corridors of the Department of State Affairs, first to Fu Hong, then to Fu Jian. The crown prince had not yet regained his authority to preside over its affairs. He received her petition and merely instructed a palace attendant to deliver it, without presuming to summon a single official. The emperor called in the officer responsible for procurement and laid Deng’s note beside the earlier, duly sealed contracts.
“Does the court owe nothing merely because there is no official seal?” Fu Jian asked.
The official knelt. “If we acknowledge this one note, a thousand shops in the South Market will come for payment tomorrow.”
“Leave the thousand shops aside. Why did the Deng family dare to incur this debt?”
“They were tempted by the officer’s promises.”
“Whose uniform was that officer wearing? Whose tally did he carry?”
Silence settled over the hall.

Fu Jian did not order the state to buy every hoard of leather in the South Market. Instead, he had the officer and the porters who had inspected the prices traced, the three cartloads of sample boots delivered from the shop to the barracks brought out, and the quantities prepared and actually received counted. For goods the army had genuinely asked to have made ready, the court would take half at a verifiable cost and use them first to make up the shortage of soldiers’ old boots. Merchandise stockpiled for private profit could not be passed off as an official order. Seven days later Madam Cao received her first wooden payment voucher. It would not cover all her debts. Still, she placed it before her dead husband’s spirit tablet, weighing down a sheaf of demands for payment.
The matter was far from over.

As the retreating army passed through Hedong, the counties sent in three wagonloads of old accounts. They recorded forty-seven government oxen lost, more than three hundred carts stuck in mud, and upward of two hundred civilian porters missing. On the third page, Fu Rong’s military clerks discovered that one cart had been entered as a loss in two different counties. They also found three porters who had died of illness in the rear camp at the Fei listed by their home districts as deserters. A magistrate hurried to blame a copying mistake. Fu Rong closed the register and told him to bring the three men’s families before he said anything more.

One of them was an old woman holding her son’s coarse jacket to her breast. Before leaving, she said, he had sewn his name into the lining, afraid that if he died in a strange land even the people collecting his body would not know what to call him.
“My lord,” she asked a military clerk, her voice hoarse, “if you write down that he ran away, where am I to go looking for him?”

An old medical register in Luoyang yielded his name. He had died of dysentery and been buried beside the road to Runan. The clerk held out the page for the woman to see. Though she could not read, she gazed at it for a long time before whispering, “So someone did remember.”

When the first Qin units returned to Chang’an, no drums or music greeted them at the gate. Crowds along the streets pressed so close that horses could scarcely pass. One woman spotted a familiar cloak and ran after a cart, only to discover, when she reached it, that it covered another man’s body. A soldier’s father seized his arm and demanded to know why, if no battle had been fought, his eyes were sunk so deep in his face. Young officers heard people mutter, “All that marching for nothing,” and more than once reached for their swords before their comrades restrained them.
Beneath the gate, an old soldier showed a clerk the crack across the sole of his shoe. “The road was real enough.”
The clerk replied only, “Under the old military code, rank is awarded for enemy killed or captured. You have none to your credit.”
The veteran looked up at the wall before him. After a while he lowered his foot and said nothing.

Fu Pi sent a letter from Luoyang asking that the returning army be credited with service in the field, to quiet the troops. His petition was urgent in tone and included the names of officers requesting another advance south. Fu Jian passed it to Fu Rong. Marching distances, length of service, wounds, and sickness could all be verified from the rolls and compensated, Fu Rong said, but titles granted for victories should not be awarded on false pretenses. Fu Pi was not present in the Chengming Hall. In his reply he wrote a single line: If the hardships of soldiers are wholly severed from military merit, who will obey an order to march far from home again?

Fu Jian summoned the officials responsible for public expenditure to discuss rewards for service on the march. Lamps were lit early outside the hall, their yellow flames enclosed in silver shades. An official began reciting the sum required; halfway through the figure, even he fell silent. Revenues from the state salt and iron works had already been shifted once the previous year to provision the assembly. Now horses had to be fed back to health, sick soldiers sent home, and granaries in the Yellow and Luo River region repaired before spring.
“Get the men home first,” Fu Jian said.
“And their reward money?”
“Pay half of what is due now. Verify and disburse the balance in installments. If payment is delayed, record the delay and the reason for it.”
“Some provinces cannot raise even half,” the official replied.

“Have each province report its shortfall. The palace will buy no new furnishings this year, and the winter grants to the imperial clan will be reduced. If that is still not enough, we shall discuss it again.”

He spoke slowly. At first those in the hall expected the emperor to produce some ingenious scheme that would refill the treasury at a stroke. Only after a long silence did they understand that he had none.

The lights of the Department of State Affairs burned deep into the night. Names in the ledgers were duplicated or missing; seals were checked one by one until the clerks’ fingers were stained red with sealing clay. Those who had died protecting the sick or holding the rear route were entered in one register; those killed in battle, in another. Missing men were no longer to be called deserters without inquiry, and their families could appeal with proof from fellow travelers. The army offices and the provinces argued for three days over the single character meaning “dead.” Fu Hong sent over an old service voucher, bearing only the name of a village and half a blurred seal.
“This belonged to the old woman’s son,” the crown prince told the clerk sent to collect it. “If even this is rejected, every man who lost his wooden token on the march will become nameless.”

The clerk knew the crown prince lacked the authority to issue a fresh order, and carefully placed the voucher in a box. The next day Fu Jian read the proposed revision and saw the few lines his son had added in his own hand. He neither summoned him to the palace nor sent the paper back.
Harder to settle than questions of grain or money was the humiliation of those who had marched.

At a grand audience before winter, Fu Shao of the imperial clan stepped forward with an impeachment jointly signed by several officers. He asked that the “ministers who had brought the realm to grief” be held to account. He had lost comrades at Wei Bridge, and the old scar on his face reddened in cold weather. He spoke with the bluntness of a man who had lived among soldiers.
“Your Majesty ordered us south, yet at the Fei would not let us fight a single battle. Now we return, and the markets say we were defeated. From whom are our soldiers to demand an explanation?”

Some blamed the crown prince and the obstruction of the three seals. Others blamed Fu Rong’s excessive caution. Others still said Murong Chui’s repeated warnings of unrest in Hebei had only planted doubts in the emperor’s mind. Murong Chui stood in the ranks, neither begging pardon nor rushing to defend himself.

Fu Jian ordered the Secretariat to bring his own decrees. From the assembly at Luoyang to the movements beyond the Ru River and finally the division of the camps for the northward withdrawal, every marginal instruction beside them had been written in his hand.
“Fu Shao,” he asked, “you have been a soldier. Whoever has the power to order men onto a road must bear the cost when that road proves wrong. Whom do you ask me to punish now?”
Fu Shao bowed his head, though his knuckles remained tense.

“You want another battle. I know.” Fu Jian paused. “I wanted one then as well. But the crown prince said the accounts did not tally; the central command said the wagons could not get through; the Duke of Yangping said the rear ranks would jam as soon as they moved. If their words displeased me, and I killed the men who spoke them, who would ever dare bring me bad news again?”
Fu Shao slowly knelt. “Your servant would not ask for their deaths. I ask only that Your Majesty not call this campaign a success.”

Fu Jian did not order the historians to record the withdrawal as a victory. He permitted them to enter its costs, deaths from illness, disorders in the camps, and resentment over unpaid relief, together with his own decision. When Fu Shao left the hall, Fu Rong followed him beneath the eaves. They stood together for a while. Then Fu Shao said abruptly, “The blood at the bridge still feels warm, yet not a drop of the Fei was reddened. I know that is a good thing. Why, then, does it taste so bitter?”
“When the men who came back alive have received their grain and pay,” Fu Rong said, “ask them what they think.”
Another matter, meanwhile, had followed the courier road from the Fei back to Chang’an.

Zhu Xu still resided in the city as a minister of Jin. Two military envoys separately testified that someone had tried to persuade him to spread false news during the Qin withdrawal. Guards traced a messenger who had disappeared along the route. Letters hidden within the wall of his family home spoke of “our lord’s former intentions” and “when the great army marches south,” and listed relay posts used by former adherents in the Qiang lands and Hebei. The hands were different. None of the letters bore Yao Chang’s signature.
After reading the file, Fu Rong went to the Chengming Hall. Remnants of snow clung to his soles; a line of faint wet prints followed him across the imperial paving.

“These men were discussing how to make the vanguard retreat at the wrong moment and the rear army fall into disorder,” he said. “Had they succeeded, would Chang’an be debating rewards for marching today?”
“Who received an order directly from Yao Chang?” Fu Jian asked.
Fu Rong shook his head. For an instant he nearly lost his restraint. “Brother, would men plotting so deeply put their own names on the paper?”
“You believe him guilty.”
“I believe that if we take no precautions, we shall one day pay for it with more lives.”

Fu Jian ordered Yao Chang summoned. Long deprived of military command, Yao retained only the title of Minister of Ceremonies. He entered with spotless cuffs and, seeing the letters on the desk, glanced first at Fu Rong.

Fu Jian questioned him in turn about Zhu Xu’s envoys, his old Qiang followers, and messages sent from the Fei. Yao admitted keeping in touch with former associates and urging the southern advance, but denied ordering any disruption of the army.
“The men writing these letters call you their lord,” Fu Rong said.
“Others decide what to call me,” Yao Chang replied. “Am I to stop the wind blowing through Chang’an, or the tongues of men in the Qiang lands?”
“If I keep you in the capital under investigation,” Fu Jian asked, “what would you say?”
Yao Chang clasped his hands. “First tell me, Your Majesty, what crime is being investigated.”

Both brothers fell silent for a moment. At length Fu Jian had the Secretariat read out the order: Yao Chang was relieved of his office as Minister of Ceremonies; all his command tallies were to be surrendered; he was to reside in a separate house in the capital pending inquiry, with his movements and letters examined and visits from implicated former followers forbidden. Evidence bearing on treason would be reviewed by the Court of Justice. His relatives were not to be held as hostages, nor the innocent implicated on account of their Qiang origin. The imperial guard would take precautions and report the investigation’s progress to court each month. The order was not to be treated as a verdict of guilt.
Yao Chang did not once protest that he had been wronged. Before leaving, he looked at Fu Jian and suddenly asked, “When Your Majesty saved my life years ago, did you ever imagine this day?”
“Then it was you I saved,” Fu Jian said. “Today it is you against whom I must take precautions.”
Yao lowered his head and smiled faintly. Then he followed the guards out.

The walls of the separate residence were not high, but two new locks hung beneath the eaves. Every person who delivered vegetables or charcoal had to be registered. Yao Chang ground ink on an old inkstone, wrote two characters, and slowly wiped them away. The guard on duty could not tell what he was doing. He only heard Yao ask whether the snow in the markets had begun to fall thickly.
“Not yet,” the guard said. “Chang’an has had only its first snowfall.”
Outside, a grain cart rumbled past and crushed the thin ice at the roadside. Yao Chang laid down his brush and sat motionless beside the window.

That same night, the Expenditure Office sent the final batch of still-unverified service-reward registers into the palace. Fu Jian turned to the last page and saw how many entries remained blank. He did not ask anyone to fill the spaces with phrases praising the army’s might. Instead he told the clerks to circle each blank and leave it for the units returning to their camps to verify.

Wind slipped through a crack in the window, rustling the corners of the papers. A servant approached with a brazier; Fu Jian waved him away. The lamplight was dim and yellow. Military account books lay one atop another, stretching across the desk to the window.

He remembered Fu Pi staring toward the southern bank that day, unwilling to look away. At his son’s age, had someone urged him to turn his horse around, he too might have felt it the deepest humiliation.
Fu Jian opened the topmost register. Beside an empty space for a name, he wrote two characters: To Verify.
